papers.title: Ruthenium Coordination Architecture Redirects Imiquimod Antiviral Activity
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.765078 v1

summary.one_liner: A Ru(II)-arene coordination complex of the TLR7 agonist imiquimod (lead trinuclear compound 7) shows anti-HSV-1/HSV-2 activity in cells and patient-derived ectocervical organoids, and transcriptomic and proteomic profiling suggests it restores interferon-responsive antiviral programmes.
summary.plain: Imiquimod is a drug that boosts the immune system and is already used to treat some skin conditions. This paper attaches it to a metal-containing structure (ruthenium) and tests the resulting compounds against herpes simplex viruses. The lead compound reduced virus activity in lab-grown cells and in human tissue models taken from the cervix, and it appeared to help restore the tissue's own virus-fighting signals that the infection had switched off.
summary.why: Herpes viruses are common and some strains resist existing antiviral drugs, so new approaches that work through the host's defences are of interest. The text supports the claim that metal coordination changes what imiquimod does, but it is an early-stage study, and the text does not show whether this would be safe or effective in people.
summary.background:
- Imiquimod: an immune-stimulating drug that activates TLR7, a sensor on immune cells that triggers antiviral responses.
- Interferons: signalling proteins the body releases to alert neighbouring cells to viral attack.
- Ruthenium(II)-arene complexes: metal-based molecules in which a ruthenium atom is bound to an aromatic ring and to other chemical groups; coordination chemistry studies how such metal centres bind and reshape drugs.
- Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1, HSV-2): common viruses causing cold sores and genital herpes; resistant strains complicate treatment.
- Organoids: small lab-grown tissue models derived from patient cells, used here to mimic cervical epithelium.
- Transcriptomics and proteomics: measuring which genes are switched on (RNA) and which proteins are present, to see how cells respond.
- Host-directed therapy: treatments that act on the body's own defences rather than directly on the virus.

papers.abstract: Immune agonists can reinforce antiviral defence, but therapeutic efficacy requires control over the magnitude and quality of the host response. Here we show that metal coordination can reprogramme the pharmacology of imiquimod, a clinically used TLR7 agonist. A series of Ru(II)-arene-imiquimod complexes identified the trinuclear compound 7 as a lead with activity against Herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 (HSV-1 and HSV-2), including clinical isolates and antiviral-resistant strains. Compound 7 directly reduced HSV-1 infectivity and broadly suppressed viral protein accumulation in infected fibroblasts. In patient-derived human ectocervical organoids, it reduced epithelial infection and the recovery of infectious virus. Transcriptomic and proteomic profiling showed that 7 selectively restored infection-suppressed interferon-responsive and antiviral restriction programmes. Thus, Ru coordination does not simply enhance imiquimod activity but redirects its pharmacology, coupling virus-directed activity to restoration of epithelial antiviral defence. These findings establish a broader principle: coordination chemistry can engineer the response profile of immune-active anti-infective agents and expand the design space of host-directed antiviral therapeutics.

papers.title: High Throughput Screening Of FDA Approved Drugs As Potential Agonist Of Mu-Opioid Receptor
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.24.769065 v1

summary.one_liner: A high-throughput screen of 1,875 FDA-approved drugs for inhibition of cAMP signalling at the human mu-opioid receptor in CHO cells identified six hits, but naloxone-sensitivity and beta-arrestin2 follow-up showed that most did not appear to act through the receptor itself.
summary.plain: Researchers searched a library of approved drugs for ones that might switch on the mu-opioid receptor, the cell-surface target of painkillers like morphine. They tested drugs in mixtures, then one at a time, and measured a chemical messenger (cAMP) inside engineered cells. Most of the apparent hits did not behave like true receptor activators when a blocking drug (naloxone) was added, so the authors caution against trusting such hits without further checks.
summary.why: Repurposing existing drugs for pain relief could be faster than developing new ones, but screening assays can pick up effects that are unrelated to the target receptor. The paper is a useful example of why extra receptor-specific tests are needed before claiming a drug acts on that receptor or is "biased" toward one signalling pathway. The text does not show any clinical implication.
summary.background:
- Mu-opioid receptor (MOR): a protein on nerve cells that opioid painkillers bind to.
- Agonist: a molecule that activates a receptor; antagonist: one that blocks it.
- Naloxone: a drug that blocks opioid receptors; if a compound's effect is cancelled or shifted by naloxone, that suggests it works through the receptor.
- cAMP: a small signalling molecule inside cells; opioid receptor activation usually lowers it. The assay measured this drop, using a light-producing sensor.
- Forskolin: a chemical used to raise cAMP first, so that inhibition can be seen.
- Beta-arrestin2 recruitment: a second, separate receptor signalling readout, used here as an orthogonal check.
- DAMGO: a standard synthetic opioid used as the reference agonist.
- EC50/potency (nM): the concentration needed for a half-maximal effect; lower means more potent.
- Repurposing / deconvolution: testing known drugs for new uses, and working back from mixtures to find the individual active compound.

papers.abstract: The mu-opioid receptor (MOR) remains an important analgesic target, but the interpretation of ligand-directed signalling preferences requires discrimination between receptor-dependent responses and effects on downstream assay readouts. We screened a library of 1,875 drug compounds for inhibition of forskolin-stimulated cyclic AMP (cAMP) accumulation in Chinese hamster ovary cells expressing human MOR and a GloSensor reporter. Primary screening of compound mixtures identified 17 active wells containing 204 compounds. Deconvolution yielded nine initial hits, six of which produced interpretable concentration-response relationships: niclosamide, sanguinarine, hexachlorophene, ataluren, altrenogest and nitazoxanide. Five of the six showed maximal cAMP inhibition of 77-80% in the initial concentration-response experiment, compared with 81 +/- 6% for DAMGO; sanguinarine had a lower maximum (24 +/- 6%). All six were less potent than DAMGO. In antagonist experiments, 300 nM naloxone shifted DAMGO potency from 0.3 to 224 nM. Of the tested compounds, only altrenogest showed a statistically significant naloxone-associated shift (367 to 905 nM; P = 0.0117). Altrenogest produced no detectable beta-arrestin2 recruitment under the PathHunter assay conditions, whereas DAMGO produced a concentration-dependent response. Thus, most cAMP hits did not show evidence of naloxone-sensitive MOR activation, and altrenogest showed a limited but measurable antagonist-sensitive component. These results highlight the importance of orthogonal receptor-dependence testing before assigning MOR agonism or signalling bias to repurposing hits.

papers.title: A scalable method for preparation and long-term preservation of tea leaf plant-derived vesicles in tissue regeneration and drug encapsulation
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.766803 v1

summary.background:
- Extracellular vesicles: tiny membrane-bound particles that cells release and that can carry molecules between cells.
- Plant-derived vesicles (PDVs): the same kind of particles obtained from plants, often proposed as cheaper, more sustainable alternatives.
- Ultracentrifugation: spinning samples at very high speed to separate particles by size and density.
- Size-exclusion chromatography (SEC): passing a sample through a column so that particles separate by size; smaller contaminants are retained longer.
- Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and endothelial cells: cell types involved in tissue repair and in lining blood vessels, used here as test cells.
- Staurosporine: a chemical that triggers cell death, used to test whether a sample protects cells.
- Quercetin: a plant compound studied as a model drug.
- Cryopreservation: storing samples at very low temperature, here -80 °C, often with protective additives such as trehalose or sucrose.
summary.one_liner: This study optimizes isolation (ultracentrifugation vs. size-exclusion chromatography), in vitro regenerative activity, quercetin loading, and six-month -80 °C storage of tea-leaf-derived plant vesicles (Tea PDVs) for tissue regeneration and drug delivery.
summary.plain: Plant cells release tiny fat-walled bubbles called vesicles, and researchers are exploring them as natural carriers for medicines. This paper compared several plants and found tea leaves gave the most vesicles and the cleanest preparations, and that a column-based separation method removed more protein contamination than the standard spinning method. The tea vesicles did not harm human cells in laboratory tests, appeared to help cells survive stress and heal and form tubes, and carried the drug quercetin better when treated with a soap-like agent.
summary.why: Vesicles that are cheap to grow, easy to scale up, and stable in storage would matter for making plant-based therapies practical. The work is laboratory-only (cell cultures and one proof-of-concept drug), so its clinical relevance is still unknown and the text does not show animal or patient data.

papers.abstract: Plant-derived vesicles (PDVs) are emerging as sustainable nanotherapeutic platforms, although challenges regarding isolation, scalability, biological activity, drug loading, and storage stability hinder their biomedical translation. This study aimed to optimize PDV production, exploring different sources to assess the one with greater translation potential, in terms of for yield and purity. To that end, PDVs from tea and red cabbage leaves, as well as ginger and turmeric roots were isolated by differential ultracentrifugation and size-exclusion chromatography (SEC), comparing both methodologies. Tea provided the highest vesicle yield and purity, with SEC outperforming ultracentrifugation in reducing soluble protein contamination. SEC isolated tea leaf-derived PDVs (Tea PDVs) were therefore further optimization using scalable fast protein liquid chromatography. Proteomic characterization showed enrichment in hydrolases, which could be related to an inherent capacity to induce tissue remodelling. Hence, regenerative potential was tested in vitro on mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and endothelial cells (HAECs). Firstly, Tea PDVs showed no cytotoxicity in MSCs and HAECs, even at high concentrations. Importantly, they significantly attenuated staurosporine-induced MSC death and promoted endothelial wound closure and capillary-like network formation, supporting their regenerative potential. Drug delivery potential was also assayed using quercetin, as a proof-of-concept drug. Saponin-mediated permeabilization significantly improved quercetin loading compared with passive incubation. Another important hurdle towards clinical translation, is determination of the ideal storage conditions for PDVs, which is still missing. To address this, we performed a six-months storage study at -80 C, analysing different cryopreservatives. The results showed that PBS alone caused substantial particle loss and increased vesicle size, whereas HEPES + trehalose-, sucrose-, and trehalose + human albumin-containing cryoprotective formulations preserved vesicle size and mitigated particle loss, facilitating long-term stability. Overall, these findings identify Tea PDVs as promising biocompatible nanocarriers with intrinsic regenerative properties. The optimized isolation, drug-loading, and preservation strategies provide a foundation for further development of plant-based nanotherapeutics targeting tissue regeneration and drug delivery applications in regenerative medicine.

papers.title: Evaluation of sources of variability in a TEER (trans-epithelial/endothelial electrical resistance) system
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.06.764605 v1

summary.background:
- TEER (trans-epithelial/endothelial electrical resistance): an electrical resistance reading across a cell layer; higher values generally indicate a tighter barrier.
- Cell inserts: small cup-like membranes on which cells are grown, letting researchers measure across the layer.
- Gut co-culture model: a lab model in which two cell types are grown together to mimic the intestinal lining.
- KCl and blank inserts: control measurements. KCl is a salt solution used as a reference reading; blank inserts have no cells and show the baseline.
- Run: a batch of plates measured in one session.
- Bayesian analysis: a statistical method that estimates how much each source of variation contributes, with uncertainty.
- Correlation: a measure of whether two sets of deviations move together; here, whether control deviations track model deviations within a run.
summary.one_liner: A case study of a chamber-based TEER system used with a gut co-culture model, analyzing 23 twenty-two-day experiments to separate within-run from run-to-run variability using Bayesian analysis and correlation of control measurements.
summary.plain: Scientists grow layers of cells on small porous inserts and measure how electrically resistant the layer is, as a way to check that it forms a tight barrier. This paper asks how much of the variation in those readings comes from within a single test session versus from one session to the next. The authors found that variation within a session was small, but differences between sessions, even ones run hours apart on the same day, were larger.
summary.why: Barrier measurements like this are used in drug testing and bioassays, so knowing where the noise comes from helps decide how results should be compared and analyzed. The text suggests the methods could be applied to other TEER measurements, though its scope is a single case study.

papers.abstract: Trans-epithelial/endothelial electrical resistance (TEER) measurements are a key nondestructive measurement of the barrier integrity of cells grown on inserts. To support the use of TEER measurements in bioassays, we have evaluated the sources of variability in a case study involving a chamber-based TEER system to assess a gut co-culture model. Data from 23 separate experiments, each lasting 22 d, were evaluated. Multiple lines of evidence suggested minimal variability within a run, a period during which several plates were analyzed sequentially. In contrast, run-to-run variability was substantially larger, even when two runs were performed several hours apart on the same day. Bayesian analysis of both KCl and blank insert data revealed that run-to-run variability was among the largest sources of variability, with relative uncertainty values of 3 % to 6 % of the mean value. Correlational analysis investigated whether deviations of KCl or blank insert TEER values within a run compared to long-term median values were correlated with deviations of the biculture gut model values within that same run from their long-term median values. Unexpectedly, the KCl values were not correlated, while the blank insert values had a weak correlation. We also evaluated the information gained from different control measurements. The findings from this study can influence how statistical analyses are performed on TEER results and can inform the design of robust TEER methods. For example, the approaches described here can be used to characterize variability within and among runs in TEER measurements for other methods.

papers.title: Lipid nanoparticle-delivered Cas13b ribonucleoproteins targeting survivin overcome gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767627 v1

summary.background:
- Gemcitabine: a standard chemotherapy drug for pancreatic cancer; tumor cells can become resistant to it.
- Survivin (BIRC5): a protein that blocks programmed cell death (apoptosis); it is often overexpressed in pancreatic tumors.
- RNA silencing: reducing how much of a specific protein a cell makes by destroying its messenger RNA.
- Cas13b: a bacterial enzyme that can be guided to cut specific RNA molecules; "ribonucleoprotein" (RNP) means the enzyme is delivered pre-bound to its guide RNA.
- Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs): tiny fat-based carriers that deliver molecules into cells; ionizable lipids help them load and release cargo.
- Xenograft: human cancer cells grown as tumors in mice, used to test treatments before human trials.
- Encapsulation efficiency: the share of the cargo that is successfully packed inside the particles.
summary.one_liner: Preassembled Cas13b ribonucleoproteins delivered in ionizable lipid nanoparticles silence BIRC5 (survivin) RNA transiently in pancreatic cancer cells and, in a PANC-1 xenograft model, combine with gemcitabine to slow tumor growth.
summary.plain: Pancreatic cancer is very hard to treat, partly because tumors stop responding to the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine. This study packaged a molecular "scissors" protein complex (Cas13b, which cuts a specific messenger RNA) inside fatty nanoparticles, then used it to switch down a survival gene called survivin. In lab cells and in mice with pancreatic tumors, switching down survivin together with gemcitabine slowed tumor growth more than either alone, according to the authors.
summary.why: Gemcitabine resistance is a central problem in pancreatic cancer, and the paper offers a proof-of-concept way to pair an RNA-targeting tool with chemotherapy. Because the silencing is meant to be transient, it may suit safer, temporary treatments, but the text is a single preclinical study in one xenograft model, so clinical relevance is unproven.

papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest cancers, largely due to its poor response to chemotherapy and the development of drug resistance. Survivin (BIRC5), an inhibitor of apoptosis frequently overexpressed in PDAC, contributes to tumor cell survival and gemcitabine resistance, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Here, we developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based platform for the delivery of preassembled spCas13b ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) to achieve transient and sequence-specific RNA silencing in pancreatic cancer cells. We optimized ionizable lipid formulations for Cas13b RNP encapsulation and identified a formulation achieving approximately 80% encapsulation efficiency, with sustained colloidal stability and gene-silencing activity during seven days of storage at 4{degrees}C. LNP-delivered Cas13b RNPs efficiently silenced endogenous BIRC5 in three pancreatic cancer cell lines, reducing survivin protein levels and inducing apoptosis. In gemcitabine-resistant PANC-1 cells, BIRC5 silencing synergistically enhanced the cytotoxic effect of gemcitabine in vitro. This therapeutic combination was further evaluated in a PANC-1 xenograft model, where only the combined administration of BIRC5-targeting Cas13b RNP-LNPs and gemcitabine significantly inhibited tumor growth, without apparent systemic toxicity. Intratumoral administration also restricted nanoparticle distribution to the injected tumors. These findings establish LNP-mediated delivery of Cas13b RNPs as a new strategy for transient RNA-targeted therapy and provide proof of concept for combining survivin silencing by Cas13b with chemotherapy to address gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer.

papers.title: Native-like 3D colonoids reveal mechanisms of colonic drug disposition
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766943 v1

summary.background:
- Organoids: small 3D clusters of cells grown in a dish from stem cells that mimic parts of an organ.
- Colonoid: an organoid grown from colon tissue.
- ADME-T: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity, the body's handling of a drug.
- Transporters (P-gp, BCRP) pump drugs in or out of cells; enzymes (CYP3A4, UGT1A, SULT1A) chemically modify drugs.
- Apical vs basal-out: whether the cells' inner-facing or outer-facing surface is exposed to the liquid around them.
- Microvilli: tiny projections on intestinal cells that greatly enlarge the absorbing surface.
- Proteomics and lipidomics: measuring the sets of proteins and fats in cells.
- HEK293: a standard, simpler human cell line used as a reference.
- Fic: intracellular bioavailability, the fraction of a drug that is free to reach targets inside cells.
summary.one_liner: Establishes adult colonic stem-cell-derived 3D organoids (colonoids) as a more native-like model for studying how drugs are absorbed, metabolised and transported in the large intestine, and links microvillar surface architecture to intracellular drug availability.
summary.plain: Drug researchers have mostly studied how medicines pass through the small intestine using lab-grown mini-organs, and the large intestine (colon) has received much less attention. This paper grows colon mini-organs from adult stem cells and compares them with real colon tissue and with cells taken directly from it. The authors report that the cells taken from tissue were a better reference than the tissue itself, and that certain mini-organ setups matched that reference most closely.
summary.why: Colon drug handling matters for oral medicines and for predicting how drugs behave in the body, and better lab models could make such predictions more reliable. The finding that the shape of the cell surface (microvilli, the tiny finger-like projections) affects how drugs enter cells may be relevant to drug design, though the text alone does not show how far this extends to patients.

papers.abstract: Intestinal organoid research in drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADME-T) has focused predominantly on small intestinal enteroids, leaving colonic drug handling comparatively unexplored. Here, we established and characterized adult colonic stem cell-based three-dimensional (3D) organoid (colonoid) models as physiologically relevant New Approach Methodologies (NAMs). Donor-matched mucosal tissue, isolated primary epithelial cells, and 3D colonoids were characterized using global and targeted proteomics, fixed and live-cell microscopy, functional ADME-T assays and targeted lipidomics. This complementary analysis identified isolated primary epithelial cells as a more representative native epithelial reference than excised mucosal tissue. Suspended differentiated apical- and basal-out colonoid configurations more closely matched this reference across the assessed characteristics. Together, these two configurations provided access to both apical and basolateral epithelial surfaces, enabling functional studies of key drug transporters (P-gp, BCRP) and metabolizing enzymes (CYP3A4, UGT1A, SULT1A) in a native-like setting. Measurement of intracellular bioavailability (Fic), reflecting drug availability to intracellular targets, revealed lipophilicity-dependent microvillar absorption mechanisms. Hydrophilic compounds exploited the enlarged membrane surface provided by microvilli, whereas highly permeable lipophilic compounds seemingly entered only at the microvillus tips. Compared with HEK293 cells, an established reference model for Fic measurements, colonoids combined native-like epithelial geometry with higher phospholipid content and generally stronger intracellular drug binding, highlighting the importance of both architecture and cellular composition for studying colonic drug disposition. These colonoid models provide a physiologically relevant platform for investigating colonic ADME-T and reveal how microvillar architecture shapes intracellular drug bioavailability.

papers.title: Pharmacolibrary: Interoperable executable models for PK, PD and PGx derived from published evidence
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766960 v1

summary.background:
- Pharmacokinetics (PK): what the body does to a drug, such as absorption, distribution and clearance.
- Pharmacodynamics (PD): what the drug does to the body, such as its effect on a target.
- Pharmacogenomics (PGx): how a person's genes change their response to drugs.
- Executable model: a mathematical model written in software code that can be run to simulate outcomes.
- Standard formats (Modelica, FMI, SBML, CellML, MATLAB): shared file types that let models be exchanged between tools.
- Large language model (LLM): an AI system that reads and generates text; here used to extract numbers from papers.
- Open-weight model: an AI model whose trained parameters are publicly released, so it can be run locally.
- Provenance tracking: recording where each piece of data came from.
summary.one_liner: Pharmacolibrary v26.11 is a source-traceable resource that uses a multi-agent LLM-plus-validation workflow to turn published pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic and pharmacogenomic evidence into executable models in several standard modelling formats.
summary.plain: Knowledge about how drugs move through and act on the body is scattered across journal papers, databases and existing computer models, which makes it hard to reuse or check. This paper describes a system that uses AI language models to pull drug parameters out of the published literature, checks them with fixed rules, records where each value came from, and turns them into runnable simulation models with browser-based demos. The authors report only preliminary tests, which suggested that splitting extraction into several steps worked better than a single pass, and that locally run open-source models performed at least comparably to leading commercial AI models.
summary.why: Automated, auditable curation of drug data could make pharmacological models easier to reuse, compare and reproduce across research, simulation and teaching. The evaluation is described only as preliminary, so the reliability of the extracted parameters at scale is not yet established by the text.

papers.abstract: Published pharmacological knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous scientific literature, databases, and computational models, making systematic reuse, comparison, and reproducibility difficult. We present Pharmacolibrary v26.11, a source-traceable resource that connects pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), and pharmacogenomic (PGx) knowledge with executable models, simulations, and interactive visualizations. A multi-agent workflow combines LLM-assisted literature retrieval and extraction with deterministic validation, ontology mapping, provenance tracking, automated model generation, and rule-based review. The system transforms published evidence and extracted parameters into executable models across Modelica, FMI, SBML, MATLAB, and CellML and provides browser-based simulations for research and education. Preliminary evaluation indicates that decomposing literature extraction into multiple stages improves parameter recovery compared with single-pass extraction and that locally deployed open-weight models can provide performance that is at least comparable with frontier commercial LLMs. Pharmacolibrary provides a foundation for scalable, auditable curation of pharmacological knowledge and for connecting published evidence to reusable computational models across research, simulation, and education.

papers.title: Nose-to-Brain Delivery of Cocaine in Mice: A Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Model Incorporating Olfactory Epithelial Transport, Mucociliary Clearance, and Blood-Brain Barrier Permeability
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.766260 v1

summary.background:
- Intranasal (IN) dosing means drug is absorbed through the nose; intravenous (IV) means injected into a vein.
- Pharmacokinetics describes how a drug is absorbed, distributed, and cleared by the body over time.
- PBPK models are equations representing real body compartments (blood flow, tissue volumes, barriers) so that parameters have physical meaning.
- The olfactory epithelium is the smell-sensing lining high in the nose, which has nerve connections to the brain and a route around the bloodstream.
- The blood-brain barrier is a layer of cells that limits which substances pass from blood into brain tissue.
- Mucociliary clearance is the nose's natural sweeping of mucus, which removes material from the nasal lining.
- Plasma protein binding refers to drug molecules attached to blood proteins, which reduces the free drug available to move into tissues.
- Tandem mass spectrometry is a lab method for measuring small amounts of a specific molecule in tissue or blood.
summary.one_liner: A physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model, fitted to mouse brain and plasma cocaine data after intranasal versus intravenous dosing, estimates how much cocaine reaches the brain via the olfactory epithelium rather than the bloodstream.
summary.plain: Snorted cocaine produces fast effects on the brain even though it leaves less cocaine in the blood than an injected dose. This paper asks how much of the brain's cocaine arrives directly through the nose, along the smell-sensing tissue, rather than through the blood. The authors measured cocaine levels in the brain and blood of awake mice given either route, then built a detailed mathematical model of the nose, blood, and brain to fit those measurements.
summary.why: The authors report that the olfactory route accounts for about half of the cocaine reaching the brain after intranasal dosing, which they suggest may explain how quickly nasal cocaine acts. This is a single animal study described only through its abstract, so the estimate depends on the model's assumptions, and its relevance to human drug use is not established by the text.

papers.abstract: Intranasal (IN) cocaine produces rapid central nervous system (CNS) effects despite generating substantially lower plasma concentrations than equivalent intravenous (IV) doses, suggesting a direct nose-to-brain pathway. The olfactory epithelium provides anatomical continuity for cocaine to pass between the nasal cavity and the brain. Quantifying the relative contribution of this pathway to total brain cocaine exposure requires a physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model that explicitly accounts for nasal mucosal architecture, epithelial transport barriers, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability. Here we used tandem mass spectrometry to collect cocaine concentration-time data from the brain and plasma of awake mice administered IV or IN cocaine and leveraged that data to generate such a framework. Our results provide evidence that following IN cocaine, the olfactory pathway accounts for approximately half of the cocaine that reaches the brain. The mechanistic PBPK framework developed here, incorporating anatomically grounded nasal compartment separation, blood-flow-scaled mucosal absorption, tissue diffusion resistance, mucociliary clearance, plasma protein binding, and BBB permeability-surface area transport, substantially improves upon empirical one-compartment absorption models and produces parameter estimates with physiological interpretability. The proportionate efficiency of the olfactory route relative to systemic absorption may provide a pharmacokinetic basis for the rapid onset of IN cocaines CNS effects and has direct implications for understanding the psychoactive effects of cocaine.

papers.title: The activation-deactivation cycle of human PIEZO1
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.766215 v1

summary.background:
- PIEZO1 is a mechanically gated ion channel: physical force on the cell membrane opens it, letting positively charged ions flow.
- Conductance (in picosiemens, pS) measures how easily current flows through an open channel.
- Membrane tension and curvature are physical stresses on the cell membrane that influence channel opening.
- Coarse-grained simulations use simplified particles for speed; atomistic simulations model every atom and are more detailed.
- A salt bridge is an attraction between oppositely charged amino acid side chains that can hold parts of a protein together.
- Yoda1 is a small molecule that activates PIEZO1; its binding site is the focus of the pharmacology claims.
summary.one_liner: Coarse-grained and atomistic simulations of human PIEZO1 in a curved, tension-controlled membrane reconstruct its gating cycle, linking a pore-lipid salt bridge, disease variants and the yoda1 binding pocket.
summary.plain: PIEZO1 is a protein channel in cell membranes that opens when the membrane is stretched or bent, letting ions pass. This paper uses computer simulations to replay the opening and closing of the channel at atomic detail, under controlled membrane tension and a physiological voltage. The authors report that the channel flattens as it activates, that the ion flow in their model matches the measured conductance of 36 pS, and that a single salt bridge helps explain two disease-linked variants.
summary.why: PIEZO1 is involved in inflammation and red blood cell volume control, so a structural account of how it switches on and off may matter for drug design. The text suggests the work offers a framework for structure-based design of modulators, but this is a simulation study and its predictions would need experimental testing.

papers.abstract: PIEZO1 is a cation channel that is primarily activated through mechanical force, and activation has been shown to be influenced by membrane curvature. PIEZO1 is ubiquitously expressed and plays critical roles in various patho-/physiological processes such as inflammatory diseases or red blood cell volume regulation. Here we combine coarse-grained and atomistic simulations in which human PIEZO1 is embedded in a curved membrane and subjected to simulations under controlled membrane tension and a physiological transmembrane potential, allowing the gating cycle to be reconstructed at atomic resolution. Systematic pressure adaptation identifies an activation regime in which the channel flattens progressively, and ion permeation quantitatively reproduces the experimental conductance of 36 pS. Furthermore, the R2456-E2117 salt bridge couples pore lipid retention to the anchor domain and disrupting it reproduces the phenotypes of the disease-associated R2456H and R2456C variants. PIEZO activation is transmitted through an interconnected network of contact rearrangements that ultimately reshapes the yoda1 binding pocket at the THU8/THU9 interface. This state-dependent remodelling rationalises the pharmacology of yoda1 and offers a framework for the structure-based design of PIEZO1 modulators.
